name: Alhambra
info: The Alhambra is a palace and fortress complex in Granada, begun in 1238 by Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, founder of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada, and the only well-preserved palace of the medieval Islamic world.

facts.made: The Nasrid sultans of Granada, from Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar (1238) to the great works of Isma'il I, Yusuf I and Muhammad V; court poet-viziers such as Ibn al-Jayyab, Ibn al-Khatib and Ibn Zamrak; later Christian additions under Charles V
facts.form: A walled palace-city about 700-740 m long on the Sabika hill, of rammed earth, brick and plaster with pine roofs, marble columns, tile mosaic and carved stucco, with the Alcazaba fortress, the Nasrid palaces and the Palace of Charles V
facts.where: On the Sabika hill above Granada, Spain, with the Generalife nearby; objects from it are in the Alhambra Museum and the National Archaeological Museum in Madrid
facts.known: the Court of the Lions and its fountain; the Court of the Myrtles and the Hall of the Ambassadors; muqarnas domes; walls of Arabic inscriptions and poetry; Washington Irving's Tales of the Alhambra; a World Heritage Site

t: The Nasrid sultans built the Alhambra as a self-contained royal city, with its greatest palaces raised in the 14th century under Yusuf I and Muhammad V.
After the surrender of Granada in 1492 it became a royal palace of the Spanish Crown, altered and added to by Charles V.
Neglected and damaged in the 18th and 19th centuries, it drew Romantic travellers and has been restored and studied since the 19th century.
dyk: The tiles of the Alhambra contain nearly all, if not all, of the seventeen mathematically possible wallpaper groups. M. C. Escher's study of them after his visit in 1922 inspired his later work on tessellation.
ev: Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar settles in Granada and begins building the Alhambra
The main gate, the Puerta de la Justicia, is built under Yusuf I
Muhammad V builds the Palace of the Lions and gives the Comares Palace much of its final look
Muhammad XI surrenders Granada to Ferdinand and Isabella, who make the Alhambra their court
Construction begins on the Renaissance Palace of Charles V
Departing French troops blow up eight towers before the remaining fuses are disabled
Washington Irving's Tales of the Alhambra is first published
The Alhambra and Generalife are listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

sections.origins:
The Sabika hill above Granada held fortresses long before the Nasrids. A citadel, probably of Visigothic date, existed there in the 9th century, and the first reference to the Qal'at al-Hamra, the red castle, comes from the fighting of the reign of 'Abdallah ibn Muhammad (888 to 912). In the 11th century the Zirids of the Taifa of Granada had their palace on the Albaicín hill, joined to fortresses on the Sabika and Mauror hills, and their powerful Jewish administrator Samuel ibn Naghrillah built a palace with gardens on the Sabika, of which nothing remains.

After Almohad rule collapsed in 1228 and Castile took Córdoba and Seville, Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar founded the Nasrid dynasty, which ruled the Emirate of Granada as the last Muslim state of al-Andalus. Settling in Granada in 1238, he began the Alhambra that same year; an Arabic chronicle records that he marked the foundations of a castle, finished the ramparts within the year and brought water from the river. The Sultan's Canal, bringing water from the mountains to the east, turned the hill into a palace-city rather than a fortress alone.
sections.content:
In the Nasrid era the Alhambra was a city apart from Granada, with a Friday mosque, baths, streets, houses, workshops, a tannery and a water system. At its western tip stands the Alcazaba fortress; along the northern edge, overlooking the Albaicín, stood at least six palaces. The best preserved are the Mexuar, where the sultan received petitions; the Comares Palace, built round the Court of the Myrtles with its long reflecting pool and the Hall of the Ambassadors, the throne room, under a wooden dome of 8,017 pieces representing the seven heavens; the Palace of the Lions; and the Partal Palace. East of the walls lies the Generalife, a Nasrid country estate.

The Palace of the Lions, built under Muhammad V, has a courtyard ringed by single, paired and grouped columns, with the Fountain of the Lions at its centre: a basin on twelve marble lions, its rim carved with a poem by Ibn Zamrak. Its halls carry muqarnas vaults, the Hall of the Two Sisters one of more than 5,000 pieces. Throughout, the walls bear Qur'anic verses, court poetry and the Nasrid motto, there is no victor but God, some poems speaking as if the room itself addressed the reader.
sections.making:
Later Nasrid rulers continuously modified the site, and the fragile materials needed regular repair, so its exact chronology is hard to fix. Muhammad II probably built the earliest palaces of which traces survive; Muhammad III built the Partal Palace, the oldest still standing, and the main mosque, completed in 1305. Isma'il I began the official palace of the sultan and the state with the Comares Palace and the Mexuar, and Yusuf I added the Hall of the Ambassadors, the Puerta de la Justicia of 1348 and the Torre de la Cautiva. Muhammad V's reign marked the high point, with the Palace of the Lions and the Comares Façade.

Little is known of the builders, but the terms of office of the heads of the chancery, who were often also viziers, coincide with the main building phases, and three of them, Ibn al-Jayyab, Ibn al-Khatib and Ibn Zamrak, wrote much of the poetry on the walls. Walls were raised in rammed earth, lime concrete or brick and plastered, roofs and ceilings made of pine, columns and fountains of white Macael marble. Tile mosaic covered the lower walls and carved stucco the upper ones, all once painted in red, blue and gold. Courtyards were aligned north to south to catch the winter sun and shade the summer.
sections.reception:
The last sultan, Muhammad XI, surrendered Granada in January 1492 without the Alhambra being attacked, and moved his ancestors' remains from its mausoleum. Ferdinand and Isabella held court there for some months: on 31 March they signed the Alhambra Decree expelling the Jews of Spain who refused to convert, and in the Hall of the Ambassadors Christopher Columbus presented his plans, the contract for his voyage being signed on 17 April. The Tendilla family became its governors and strengthened its towers against artillery.

Charles V visited in 1526 and turned parts of the Nasrid palaces into royal apartments between 1528 and 1537. He also demolished part of the Comares Palace for a new palace designed by Pedro Machuca in the Italian Renaissance style, a building meant to show the emperor's status and the triumph of Christianity over Islam; it was begun in 1527 and left unroofed in 1637. The mosque was replaced by the Church of Santa María de la Alhambra. In Muslim societies the Alhambra was often remembered with nostalgia after 1492, and Saadian monuments in Morocco appear to imitate the Court of the Lions.
sections.survival:
Decline began after 1717 to 1718, when Philip V removed the Tendilla-Mondéjar family; the palaces fell to self-interested local governors, and early 19th-century visitors found prisoners, disabled soldiers and the poor living in them. Napoleon's troops occupied it from 1810 to 1812 and on leaving blew up eight towers before a Spanish soldier, José Garcia, disabled the remaining fuses. An earthquake in 1821 and a fire in the Sala de la Barca in 1890 caused further damage.

Restoration began in 1828 under José Contreras, followed by his son and grandson, who practised stylistic restoration and added invented features such as Persian-looking domes in the Court of the Lions. The Alhambra became a National Monument in 1870. Leopoldo Torres Balbás, chief architect from 1923 to 1936, brought a scientific approach on the lines of the 1931 Athens Charter: he reversed many inaccurate additions, roofed the Palace of Charles V and excavated lost Nasrid palaces. A Council of the Alhambra has overseen the site since 1940, under the Regional Government of Andalusia since 1984. Research and restoration continue.
sections.legacy:
From the late 18th century Spanish illustrators recorded the Alhambra, and in the 19th it became an object of fascination for Romantic writers and artists, whose work, coloured by European Orientalism, set its ornate halls against their ruin. Washington Irving, who lived in Granada in 1830, published Tales of the Alhambra in 1832, which did much to bring southern Spain's Islamic monuments to international attention; Richard Ford, Chateaubriand, John Frederick Lewis and Owen Jones made it widely known.

Owen Jones's Plans, Elevations, Sections and Details of the Alhambra, published from 1842 to 1845, helped launch the Alhambresque or Moresque style in Western building, seen in the Isaac M. Wise Temple in Cincinnati and the Villa Zorayda in Florida, and later taken up in the Ottoman Empire and in Cairo's Gezira Palace, whose interiors Jones designed. The Alhambra was one of the first Islamic monuments to be studied by modern scholarship, and M. C. Escher, after his visit in 1922, drew on the symmetries of its tiles for his work on tessellation. With the Generalife it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984 and is one of Spain's most visited places.

summary: The Alhambra is the palace-city of the Nasrid sultans of Granada, begun in 1238 and given its finest palaces in the 14th century, with courtyards, fountains, muqarnas vaults and walls of carved poetry. A Spanish royal palace after 1492, damaged and neglected in later centuries, it has been restored since the 19th century and is a World Heritage Site.
